Three weeks after Nitin ended it, Usha still slept with her phone under the pillow.

Some nights she missed him so much she replayed his old voice notes. Other nights she was so angry she drafted captions for a post about everything he had done wrong. On Thursday she caught herself opening a friend's account to see who he'd been out with, and her stomach dropped. This wasn't her.

She put the phone face down and called her cousin Gauri, who came over with samosas. "You're allowed to miss him and hate him on the same day," Gauri said. "You're not allowed to let it take over your life."

Together they muted his number and deleted the draft post. Usha asked Gauri to check in every evening that week, and she joined her college friends for badminton on Saturday.

The longing didn't vanish. But on Sunday she went a whole afternoon without checking anything.

qa.q: What did Gauri bring when she came over?
qa.a: Gauri brought samosas.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling when she caught herself opening a friend's account?
qa.a: Usha felt shocked and ashamed; her stomach dropped because checking on Nitin like that did not feel like who she was.

qa.q: Which steps helped Usha, and why?
qa.a: Muting his number, deleting the post and leaning on Gauri and friends gave Usha distance and support, protecting her and Nitin from harm.

qa.q: What would change for Nitin if Usha had published the post?
qa.a: Nitin could have been publicly shamed and hurt, and the conflict could have grown instead of ending.

grounding: Shows a young woman swinging between longing and rage after a breakup, tempted to watch and shame her ex online, and choosing no-contact and support instead.

"Look at this," Tejas said, holding out his phone. "Screenshots of every message Vasudha sent me. I'm putting them in the college group. Let everyone see who she really is."

Omkar didn't take the phone. "What happens after you post them?"

"She gets embarrassed. Like I was."

"And then?"

Tejas stared at the screen. "I don't know. I just miss her, and I hate her, and it's the same minute."

"That sounds exhausting."

"It is." His voice cracked. "I keep opening her profile at two in the morning."

"Okay. Want to try something? Delete the screenshots. Mute her everywhere. No messages, even the angry ones, for a month. And you text me at two in the morning instead."

"You'll be asleep."

"Then I'll reply at seven."

Tejas laughed, barely. He deleted the folder while Omkar watched, then muted Vasudha's account. "One month," he said. "Hold me to it."

qa.a: Tejas planned to put screenshots of every message Vasudha sent him in the college group.

It's been four months since Parul and I ended things, and my friends still want me to call her toxic. I'm Ankita, and I get why: the last half year was mostly silence and small fights about nothing.

But when I sit with it honestly, that's not the whole story. Parul was the first person who asked what I wanted and waited for the answer. She taught me to say "I need a minute" instead of storming off. She dragged me to Sunday flower markets, and I still go.

We wanted different lives. She wanted to move abroad; I wanted to stay near my family. Nobody was a villain.

Last week I found her old bookmark in a novel. I didn't throw it out and I didn't cry. I just felt a quiet thank-you, and something like letting go. I put the book back on the shelf and made tea.

qa.a: Parul took Ankita to Sunday flower markets.

qa.a: Ankita felt calm and grateful, a quiet thank-you mixed with letting go, rather than anger or grief.

qa.q: Why is Ankita's way of remembering the relationship a healthy one?
qa.a: Ankita admits the hard months but also keeps what Parul taught, so there is closure without turning Parul into a villain.

qa.q: How might Ankita's friends see the breakup differently?
qa.a: The friends seem protective and angry on Ankita's behalf, so they focus on the silence and fights and want to call Parul toxic.

grounding: Shows a young person acknowledging what a past relationship taught and letting go without rewriting the ex as a villain.

College counselling centre, follow-up note, Friday.

Rukmini came for her fourth session since the breakup with Manjula in January. In the first sessions she mostly listed what Manjula had done wrong, and she clenched her fists as she spoke.

Today was different. She brought a notebook where she had written two lists, as we had discussed: "what hurt" and "what I learned." The second list was longer than she expected. She read out, "I learned I can be loved and still be myself," and then went quiet for a while.

She said she still feels sad at their old canteen table. She has decided not to message Manjula, and also not to speak badly of her to mutual friends. "It was real. It just ended," she said.

I told her that both lists can be true at once. We agreed to meet once more in two weeks, and then as she needs.

qa.a: The lists were "what hurt" and "what I learned."

qa.a: Rukmini seemed moved and a little sad, but also grateful, since she went quiet after reading it.

In their rented room behind the Sirsa bus depot, Vikas and his cousin Simran had one rule for the first term: whoever was up first filled the water drums before the tank ran dry at seven.

By October it was always Vikas. Three mornings in a row he hauled buckets while Simran slept. He started banging the steel mugs loudly and sighing. Simran just rolled over.

On Sunday afternoon, when they were both eating jalebi on the roof and nobody was in a hurry, Vikas said, "Can I bring up the water thing? This week I filled the drums Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. I'm getting angry, and I don't want to."

Simran winced. "My alarm doesn't work before six."

"Then how about this: I do mornings, you do the evening dishes and the gas cylinder booking?"

Simran thought about it. "Deal. And I'll stop leaving pans overnight."

The mugs have been quiet since.

qa.q: When did the tank run dry?
qa.a: The tank ran dry at seven.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he banged the steel mugs and sighed?
qa.a: Vikas felt frustrated and resentful about doing the water duty alone, and was showing it indirectly.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than banging mugs, and why?
qa.a: Raising it on a calm Sunday with specific days and a proposed swap worked, because Simran could respond to facts and a fair fix instead of noise.

qa.a: Simran likely feels a little guilty and caught out, but not attacked, so she explains her alarm and agrees to the swap.

The sticky note on the fridge in the Cape Town student flat read, in Lindiwe's handwriting: "Some of us have exams. Just saying."

Jin's boyfriend had stayed over five nights out of seven, although they had agreed on two. Lindiwe had written three notes that month. Jin had answered none of them, only started leaving earlier.

On Saturday morning, over toast, Lindiwe pulled the notes off the fridge. "I'm sorry about these. They weren't fair. Can we talk properly?"

Jin put down her mug. "Okay."

"We said two nights a week. It's been five most weeks this month. I can't study in the lounge, and the bathroom's always busy at seven."

"I didn't realise it was that many," Jin said slowly.

"What if we use a shared calendar? Two nights, and you tell me a day before. And exam weeks, none."

Jin nodded. "That's fair. I'll tell him tonight."

Aadhya put her spoon down. "Mummy, I don't want to meet anyone before my thesis is done."

The week after Papa's knee operation, everyone said the same thing: "Now Lokesh will run the shop."

I'm Lokesh, and I was in the final year of architecture in Nagpur. I loved it. But every time I looked at Papa's bandaged leg, I felt like a selfish person for even wanting to go back.

Her father looked up from the newspaper. "Pune? What's wrong with a job here?"

"Nothing's wrong with here, Papa. But this is the team I want to learn from."

I told my parents about Jasleen on a Sunday morning, after Mama's prayers, because that's when the house is calmest.

I'm Yash. I had practised the words for a week. Mama had already shortlisted three families. I knew how much she and Papa had given up: the old scooter Papa kept for twelve years so I could go to college, the pilgrimage Mama postponed twice.

In the carpentry shed behind Nandgaon market, Tejas had spent two years at Anirban's side. He copied the way Anirban held a chisel, the way he tested wood with a knuckle. If a customer asked him anything, he said, "Ask Anirban-da."

Then Anirban went to his daughter's wedding for a week, and the headmaster came with a broken school bench. Tejas looked at the cracked leg and heard Anirban's voice in his head: replace it. But the wood was sound; only the joint had failed. He decided to re-glue and pin it instead, and it held.

When Anirban came back, Tejas showed him the bench, braced for a scolding. Anirban pushed on it with his full weight. "I would have replaced the leg," he said. "Your way saves the school money. Good call."

For a year at the Accra design studio, Kofi had run every decision past Chidi. Which font, which colour, whether a client email sounded polite enough. Chidi always answered, patiently, and Kofi always did exactly that.

In March a school asked for a new logo. Chidi sketched a bold shield. Kofi looked at it for a long time and felt his stomach knot. It looked like a bank, not a school for small children.

He could have just drawn the shield. Instead he made a second version: rounded letters, a small open book. At the meeting he said, "I think yours is strong, but I'm worried it feels too serious for the parents. Can I show another option?"

Chidi studied both. "You're right," she said. "Show the client yours first."

The client chose Kofi's. That evening Chidi asked his opinion on her own project, and she actually used it.

At the Pune college canteen, Himani said she supported widening the Ganeshkhind road even if it meant cutting some old trees.

Rekha laughed. "That's the stupidest thing I've heard this year. Only people who don't care about the planet think that." Himani went quiet and left early.

When I was twenty, my best friend Vasant cleared the engineering entrance. I failed it. The same evening his family distributed pedas in our lane. I ate one, hugged him, and meant it. Then I went home and cried into my pillow.

For months I couldn't decide what kind of friend I was. I was truly happy for him. I was also jealous enough to skip his farewell. Both were true.

What changed things was his first letter from college. He wrote that he was homesick and struggling in maths. I had imagined his life as perfect because mine felt bad. His timeline wasn't mine.

I took the exam again the next year and passed. We're still friends.

So, Jahnavi, be happy for Isha, be sad for yourself. Just don't race her calendar.

qa.a: Vasant's family distributed pedas in the lane.

qa.a: Chinmay felt genuinely happy for Vasant and also jealous and hurt about failing, crying into his pillow later.

qa.q: What turning point helped young Chinmay stop comparing himself with Vasant?
qa.a: Reading Vasant's letter about homesickness and struggling in maths showed that Vasant's life wasn't perfect and their timelines were different.

qa.q: How might Vasant have felt when Chinmay skipped his farewell?
qa.a: Vasant might have felt confused or hurt, missing his best friend at an important moment without knowing why.

grounding: Shows through an elder's memory how a young person can feel happy for a successful friend and pained for himself at once, and how comparing timelines is the trap.

subtopic: Friend succeeds when you are struggling
passage:
The farewell party for Pranav was at eight, and Lakshmi's online interview was at nine the next morning. She had eleven rejections in her inbox. Pranav had a job in Singapore.

She nearly didn't go. Then she thought of the three years they had studied together in the library and put on her good kurta.

At the party everyone asked about her job search. Each time, she smiled and said, "Still looking." Pranav's speech thanked "Lakshmi, who explained statistics to me twice." Her eyes stung. She was proud of him. She also wanted, very badly, to be somewhere else.

At ten she hugged him. "I'm so happy for you. I'm also a bit jealous. Is that terrible?"

"No," Pranav said. "I was jealous of you all of second year."

She laughed, went home, ironed her shirt for the morning and switched off her phone. Her interview was hers, not a race with anyone.

qa.q: At what time was Lakshmi's interview?
qa.a: Lakshmi's interview was at nine the next morning.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when Pranav thanked her in his speech?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt proud and moved for Pranav, while also envious and sad about her own struggle, wishing she could be elsewhere.

qa.q: What helped Lakshmi hold both feelings without letting envy take over?
qa.a: Naming both feelings honestly to Pranav and then focusing on her own interview instead of comparing timelines.

qa.q: How does Pranav respond to Lakshmi's honesty, and what does that show about how he sees her?
qa.a: Pranav admits he was once jealous of her too, showing he sees her as an equal friend, not someone behind him.

grounding: Shows a young woman who is struggling feeling both happiness and envy at a friend's success, and stepping away from comparing timelines.
